title: Deploys: Canary, Blue-Green, Flags
subtitle: Watch the same new version ship four ways and see how much damage a bad build can do in each.
learn: How rolling, blue-green, and canary deploys differ in cost, speed, and blast radius
Why a canary needs automatic metric checks to be worth anything
How feature flags separate deploying code from releasing a feature
What a dark launch (shadow traffic) tests that staging cannot
How expand/contract migrations keep the database safe while two versions run at once

steps.title: Shipping without breaking things
steps.body: Your team has a new build, v2, and 40 servers running v1 for millions of users. Every deploy is a bet that v2 behaves in production like it did in tests. Sometimes it loses. The real question is not how to deploy, but how many users see a bad build, and how fast you can undo it.
steps.idea: Deploy strategy is risk management: limit how many users a bad build reaches and how fast you can undo it.
steps.caption: All traffic is on v1. v2 is built and waiting.

steps.title: Rolling: swap servers in batches
steps.body: A rolling deploy replaces v1 instances with v2 a few at a time, for example 4 of 40 per batch, waiting for health checks between batches. It needs no extra capacity and is the default in most orchestrators. The catch: for the whole rollout, both versions serve traffic at once, and a bad v2 reaches users batch after batch unless a check stops it. Rolling back means rolling forward again with the old build.
steps.idea: Rolling is cheap and simple, but old and new run together and rollback is slow.
steps.caption: Router sends users to a mix of v1 and v2 instances.

steps.title: Blue-green: flip a whole environment
steps.body: Blue-green keeps two full environments. Blue (v1) serves users while green (v2) is started and smoke-tested with no real traffic. Then the router flips 100% of traffic to green in one step. Rollback is just flipping back, often within seconds, because blue is still running. The price is paying for roughly double capacity during the switch, and a flip still exposes everyone at once.
steps.idea: Blue-green gives instant rollback at the cost of double capacity and an all-at-once switch.
steps.caption: Router flips every request from v1 to v2 in one move.

steps.title: Canary: a small slice first
steps.body: A canary sends a small share of real traffic, say 5%, to v2 while 95% stays on v1. Automation then compares v2 against v1 on the same signals: error rate, p99 latency, saturation. If v2 stays within a set margin (for example errors within 0.1 points of v1) for 10 minutes, the share steps up to 25%, 50%, and 100%. Only real users reveal some bugs, so the canary hands them a small, bounded dose.
steps.idea: A canary tests v2 on real traffic while capping the blast radius, but only if the metric comparison is automatic.
steps.caption: 5% of requests reach v2; both versions are measured.

steps.title: The canary catches a bad build
steps.body: Suppose v2 has a bug that breaks 5% of its own requests. At 5% traffic the fleet-wide error rate barely moves, but v2's own error rate is 25 times v1's, and the comparison trips within two minutes. The router drops v2 to 0% automatically. Roughly 5% of users saw a few failed requests for two minutes. A blue-green flip or a full rolling deploy would have exposed everyone.
steps.idea: Small blast radius plus automatic rollback turns an outage into a blip.
steps.caption: v2 errors spike; router pulls traffic back to v1.

steps.title: Feature flags: deploy is not release
steps.body: A feature flag is a runtime on/off switch checked in code, such as if flags.enabled("new-checkout", user). You can ship v2 to every server with the feature off, then turn it on for staff, then 1% of users, then everyone, without another deploy. Turning it off takes seconds, not a rebuild. The cost: flags are extra code paths to test, and stale flags pile up, so remove each one once the rollout is done.
steps.idea: Flags decouple deploying code from releasing a feature, giving per-user control and a seconds-long kill switch.
steps.caption: v2 reads the flag service; the feature is on for a small group.

steps.title: Dark launch: run it, hide the result
steps.body: A dark launch sends a copy of live requests to v2 but throws away its responses, so users only see v1's answers. You learn how v2 handles real traffic shapes, data sizes, and load, such as whether it holds a p99 of 180 ms at production volume, with zero user risk. Guard against side effects: the shadow path must not send emails, charge cards, or write to shared data.
steps.idea: Shadow traffic tests v2 on real load with no user impact, as long as it has no side effects.
steps.caption: Requests are mirrored to v2; only v1's responses go back.

steps.title: The database must serve both versions
steps.body: In every strategy above, v1 and v2 share one database for a while, and you cannot atomically flip a schema. So change it in phases called expand/contract. Expand: add a nullable column full_name, which v1 ignores. Deploy v2, which writes both old and new columns, and backfill old rows. Switch reads to the new column. Contract: only in a later deploy, once no v1 runs and rollback is no longer needed, drop the old columns.
steps.idea: Never ship a schema change that breaks the old version; add first, migrate, and remove in a separate later deploy.
steps.caption: Both versions read and write the same database.

steps.title: Pick by blast radius and rollback speed
steps.body: Rolling is cheap but slow to undo. Blue-green undoes in seconds but costs double capacity and flips everyone. Canary limits exposure and needs good metrics. Flags give per-user control after deploy, and dark launches test load for free. Underneath all of them, expand/contract keeps the database compatible with both versions. Mature teams combine them: canary the build, flag the feature.
steps.idea: Combine canary for the build, flags for the feature, and expand/contract for the data.
steps.caption: Each tool limits risk at a different layer.

quiz.q: Your service is stateless, you have no spare capacity budget, and a few minutes of mixed versions is fine. Which strategy fits best?
options: Blue-green, because it is always safest
Rolling deploy in small batches with health checks
Dark launch to production
Canary with a full duplicate fleet
quiz.why: Rolling needs no extra capacity. Blue-green requires roughly double the servers during the switch, which this team has ruled out.

quiz.q: A canary at 5% traffic shows v2's error rate at 4% and v1's at 0.2%, but the fleet-wide error rate looks normal. What should happen?
options: Continue; the overall rate is fine
Roll back, because the comparison is v2 against v1, not the fleet average
Wait an hour for the numbers to average out
Raise the canary to 50% to get more data
quiz.why: At 5% share, a broken v2 is diluted in the fleet average. The canary only works when you compare the canary group directly against the baseline.

quiz.q: A bug is found in a new feature already live for 100% of users behind a flag. What is the fastest fix?
options: Roll the entire deploy back
Flip the flag off
Start a blue-green switch
Wait for the next release train
quiz.why: The flag decouples release from deploy, so turning it off takes seconds and needs no new build. Other unrelated changes in the deploy stay live.

quiz.q: You want to rename a column from name to full_name. Which plan is safe while v1 and v2 run together?
options: Rename it in the same deploy that ships v2
Add full_name, write both, backfill, switch reads, and drop name in a later deploy
Drop name first, then deploy v2
Take the site down and rename it
quiz.why: A direct rename breaks whichever version expects the other column name. Expand/contract keeps both versions working and delays the destructive step until rollback is no longer needed.

quiz.q: What does a dark launch tell you that a canary does not?
options: How v2 behaves under full production load with no user ever seeing its responses
Whether users like the new feature
Whether the database schema is correct
Nothing; it is the same thing
quiz.why: A dark launch mirrors traffic and discards v2's output, so users face zero risk. A canary serves real responses to a small group of users.

cheatsheet.def: Replace instances in batches with health checks between them. No extra capacity; old and new coexist; rollback is another rollout.
Two full environments; flip the router to switch. Instant rollback, about 2x capacity during the switch, all users move at once.
Send a small share (1-5%) of real traffic to the new version, compare its metrics with the old, then step up. Needs automatic checks.
How many users or requests a bad change can affect before it is stopped. Deploy strategy is mainly about shrinking this.
A runtime switch that turns code paths on per user or percentage. Decouples deploy from release; remove stale flags.
Mirror live traffic to the new version and discard its responses. Tests load and correctness with no user exposure; avoid side effects.
Schema change in phases: add new, dual-write and backfill, switch reads, drop old in a later deploy. Keeps v1 and v2 both working.
Canary the build, flag the feature, expand/contract the schema, and always know how to roll back before you start.
